newsitem.title: UK: FTSE 100 sets record closing high for second day.
newsitem.headline: FTSE 100 sets record closing high for second day.

text.p: Britain's leading share index finished at a record closing high for the second straight day on Tuesday as investors poured into banking, retail and pharmaceutical stocks that are insulated from sterling's strength.
Ignoring a weak start on Wall Street and softer gilt futures, the FTSE 100 finished up 41.9 points or 0.86 percent to 4,899.3, after reaching 4,903.2.
That leaves the next 100-point hurdle at 5,000, the consensus ceiling for year-end forecasts in a recent Reuters poll of UK share strategists.

"Investors are looking where to put their money next and having pushed the food retailers as far as they are justified, they have gone back to the old favourites," said Steve Wright, equities strategist at BZW.
"Currency sensitivity is still the key issue and international liquidity is going into the big cap stocks like banking," he said.
Yet the rally extended to the broader mid-cap FTSE 250, which posted its largest one-day gain in a month and ended 27.6 points higher at 4,451.5.
Bank shares were largely responsible for leading the FTSE 100 higher, contributing to more than half of the index's gains on a shortage of stock.
"The banks are going through the roof again. All the big stocks (heavy weightings) are moving on the upside and that's enough to carry the market," one dealer said.
"There's been a lot of talk that people should switch from equities into gilts," the dealer said. "But gilts were down sharply yesterday and equities are hitting new highs."
HSBC finished 84-1/2p higher at 20.85 stg after a strong rally in Hong Kong and as Dresdner Kleinwort Benson raised its price target for the stock to 24.00 stg.
Standard Chartered, Barclays and Lloyds TSB also fuelled the rally.
In its review of the sector, Kleinwort Benson raised its target for Lloyds share price, which ended at 695p, to 830p from 780p and upgraded Standard Chartered and Barclays to "add".
Halifax Plc and Alliance & Leicester Plc missed out on the rally. Traders blamed rich valuations and a slowdown in mortgage banking growth.
Traders said U.S. retail sales data out on Tuesday did not influence the UK market since they were focusing on a healthy domestic economy and continued high levels of cash held by institutions.
U.S. retail sales data rose 0.5 percent in June but May was revised downward to a 0.3 percent decline. Economists expected June sales to rise 0.2 percent.
Meanwhile, sterling continued to hover just under its 6-1/2 year highs against the German mark, helped by the anticipation of further domestic interest rate rises.
But figures from the British Retail Consortium showed prices in shops rose just one percent in the year to June.
Retail sales growth also eased to 4.5 percent compared with 4.8 percent in May according to the BRC.

"The interest rate scenario has seemed to cool off a bit and that is helping everybody," one dealer said. "Sterling hasn't fallen back and the exporters may be getting hurt, but it's not stopping the market powering to new highs."

Elsewhere, retail stocks and pharmaceuticals remained strong. Kingfisher and Dixons rose after the BRC said "windfall" cash from building society flotations was being spent on electrical goods, furniture and kitchen appliances.
British Telecommunications topped the most active list, falling 4-1/2p to 452p on continued worries over its merger with MCI Communications, dealers said.
BT executives braced for a grilling by alarmed shareholders at its annual meeting on Wednesday in Edinburgh, after MCI's unexpected profit warning last week.
-- John Hanley, London Newsroom +4 171 542 4366
